extensions.jp: 食べたあとで散歩します。
extensions.en: Past form, future sentence — た marks completion, not time.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The dentist's form asks what you do before bed, which is a question you can answer in English in four words and cannot answer in Japanese at all. Everything you have learned this step joins two actions in one order; this one joins them in the other.
setting.jp: 寝るまえに歯をみがきます。
setting.en: I brush my teeth before sleeping.

extensions.scene: She asks about the medicine you are on and whether you take it before food, and you build the sentence yourself out of the same joint — with the verb in front sitting in its plain, unbent, dictionary shape.
extensions.jp: 食べるまえに薬を飲みます。
extensions.en: I take the medicine before eating.

extensions.scene: Then you say something about last year, and the verb in front stubbornly refuses to go into the past even though the event plainly did. This joint takes the present regardless, and the sentence's tense lives at the very end.
extensions.jp: 日本に来る前に、日本語を勉強しました。
extensions.en: Before coming to Japan, I studied Japanese — 来る, not 来た.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Marking, forty exercise books, and the staffroom radio left on because the room is otherwise quiet enough to hear the clock on the wall. Somebody comes in and asks what you are doing, and the honest answer has two verbs in it — both belonging to the same person, across the same stretch of the same afternoon.
setting.jp: 音楽を聞きながら勉強します。
setting.en: I study while listening to music.

extensions.scene: You ask her the same about her own evenings, and the pattern goes out as easily as it came in — two things, one body, happening across the same stretch of time.
extensions.jp: 話しながら歩きました。
extensions.en: We walked while talking.

extensions.scene: You say it the other way round and change what you claimed to be doing. The verb after the joint is the main one, so the order is not decoration — it decides which activity you were actually engaged in.
extensions.jp: 勉強しながら音楽を聞きます。
extensions.en: Listening to music, with studying alongside — the priority flipped.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Monday morning and the small talk is about the weekend. You did five or six things, none in an order anyone needs, and two of them you would rather not go into. What the question wants is a flavour of two days rather than a timetable of them.
setting.jp: 週末は本を読んだり、映画を見たりします。
setting.en: At weekends I read, watch films, that sort of thing.

extensions.scene: You ask her the same back and get a list built the identical way — a sample, openly incomplete, with the honest implication that there were other things and neither of you is listing them.
extensions.jp: 音楽を聞いたり、散歩したりしました。
extensions.en: I listened to music, went for a walk, and so on.

extensions.scene: You drop the closing verb because the list already felt finished, and the sentence hangs unfinished instead. That final one is not decoration — it is carrying the tense for everything in front of it.
extensions.jp: 読んだり見たりしました。
extensions.en: The closing します/しました holds the tense for the whole list.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A character on a school form that you can see, copy and not read, in a word nobody will pronounce for you because everybody assumes you can. What you need is not the meaning but the method — and Japanese turns a verb into a way-of-doing-it by bolting one syllable onto its stem.
setting.jp: 漢字の読み方を教えてください。
setting.en: Please teach me how to read this kanji.

extensions.scene: It works on anything. The ticket machine at the station has beaten you twice, and the same construction turns using it into a noun you can ask a stranger about.
extensions.jp: 使い方がわかりません。
extensions.en: I don't know how to use it.

extensions.scene: What comes out the other end is a full noun, which means the particle in front has to change — the thing you are reading stops taking the object marker and takes the glue from Step 3 instead.
extensions.jp: 漢字の読み方がわかりません。
extensions.en: 漢字の, not 漢字を — the result is a noun.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
方 is outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed. Kept because the word is the module's own example vocabulary for this point.

setting.scene: You bought a suitcase for the move. Whether you bought it at home in the week you were packing, or in a department store three days after you landed, is a difference every listener hears — and it turns on one character in the sentence you tell it with.
setting.jp: ひまなとき、音楽を聞きます。
setting.en: When I'm free, I listen to music.

extensions.scene: You use it about your own childhood, which needs the noun version of the joint rather than the verb one — and nouns arrive at it through the same の from Step 3.
extensions.jp: 子どものとき、東京に住んでいました。
extensions.en: When I was a child, I lived in Tokyo.

extensions.scene: Then the suitcase sentence, where the tense in front is measured against the other half of the sentence rather than against now. One character decides which country the shop was in.
extensions.jp: 日本に行くとき、空港でかばんを買いました。
extensions.en: Bought on the way — this side's airport, before arrival.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
空港 uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed; kept because it is the module's own example.

setting.scene: Sports day is Saturday and the whole school is watching the forecast, because the decision to move it gets made on Friday afternoon by somebody who will ask what you think. The weather report itself never says will. It says something one notch below that, every single evening.
setting.jp: 明日は晴れるでしょう。

extensions.scene: Asked directly what you reckon, you hedge the same way about something you have no business being certain of — the shape lets you answer the question without pretending to knowledge you do not have.
extensions.en: It'll probably rain.

extensions.t: Said with the pitch rising, でしょう？ is a different move entirely — it means right?, fishing for agreement, and it is ね's pushier cousin. Falling, it hedges; rising, it presses. And だろう is the same word in plain register, common between friends.
extensions.scene: Somebody says it back to you with the tone going up at the end, and it is no longer a hedge — it is a request that you agree, which is a different thing to be handed.
extensions.jp: 明日は晴れるでしょう？
extensions.en: It'll be sunny tomorrow, right? — rising, this presses.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
晴れる sits outside the Step 7 bank; it is the module's own example verb.
晴 is outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed. Kept because the word is the module's own example vocabulary for this point.

setting.scene: A restaurant with no pictures on the menu and no English on the wall, and the question you need is not whether they will help you but whether a thing exists on the premises. Japanese has two verbs for existing and the line between them is drawn by aliveness, strictly, with no exceptions for how much you care about the thing.
setting.jp: 机の上に本があります。
setting.en: There's a book on the desk.

extensions.scene: At the next table there is a cat asleep on a chair, which is a fact about the same room needing the other verb entirely — because it is alive, and that is the only question the grammar asks.
extensions.jp: いすの上に猫がいます。
extensions.en: There's a cat on the chair.

extensions.scene: Then you ask the actual question, and the verb for existing turns out to cover having as well — which is how you ask a restaurant for an English menu without knowing the verb for have.
extensions.jp: 英語のメニューはありますか。
extensions.en: Do you have an English menu? — existence covers possession.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
英語 and メニュー sit outside the Step 8 bank; from the module's own wrinkle.
英 is outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed. Kept because the word is the module's own example vocabulary for this point.

setting.scene: The bank form has a section about what you own, which is a strange thing to be asked in a language you are still assembling. Ownership has its own verb, and it sits in the continuing form you learned in Step 4 — because owning is a state you are in rather than an action you perform.
setting.jp: 車を持っています。

extensions.scene: They ask whether you have a residence card on you, which you do, in the wallet where it has to live — the same verb, the same continuing shape, about the one object you are legally required to be carrying.
extensions.jp: カードを持っています。
extensions.en: I have my card with me.

extensions.scene: The next box asks about family, and the verb quietly refuses. People are never held — a brother is not a possession grammatically, so having one runs through the alive-existence verb instead.
extensions.en: I have an older brother — います, never 持っています.

claims: Mid-to-long-term residents aged 16 and over must carry the residence card at all times

setting.scene: Somebody at the station asks you for directions, in Japanese, on the assumption that you live here — which after four months you do. You know exactly where the bank is and cannot say it, because Japanese builds the place first and parks the thing in it afterwards.
setting.jp: 銀行は駅の前にあります。
setting.en: The bank is in front of the station.

extensions.scene: She asks about the post office too, which is behind the same building, and the second sentence comes out faster than the first because the frame is already built and only the landmark has moved.
extensions.en: The room is downstairs.

extensions.scene: The landmark comes first and the relationship second, which is the reverse of the English. 机の上 is the desk's top — a place-noun built out of two nouns, and only then does anything get parked in it.
extensions.en: It's on the desk — literally, at the desk's top.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The same question from Step 2 comes back with something new attached: is something happening here, or simply located here. What has changed is that the existence verb can now sit on either side of that line, because it has a second job — an event being held somewhere is also a thing that exists.
setting.jp: 机の上に本があります。

extensions.scene: The staffroom noticeboard says there is a party at the school tomorrow, and the same verb takes the other particle — because a party is not sitting there, it is happening there.
extensions.jp: 明日、学校でパーティーがあります。
extensions.en: There's a party at school tomorrow — happening, so で.

extensions.t: The particle follows the meaning, not the verb. あります meaning exists takes に; あります meaning takes place takes で. Same word on the page, two different jobs, and only the sense tells you which particle it wants.
extensions.scene: You write both sentences down one under the other and the verb is identical in each. Nothing on the page distinguishes them except what the sentence is claiming about the world.
extensions.jp: 部屋に机があります。学校で会議があります。
extensions.en: A desk exists in the room. A meeting happens at school.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
パーティー and 会議 sit outside the Step 8 bank; 会議 arrives in Step 12.

setting.scene: You have been ill for a week and three separate people have done something about it — one lent you a heater, one brought soup, one went to the pharmacy. Telling that story needs three different verbs for what English calls giving, and which one you pick depends on which direction the kindness travelled.
setting.jp: 友達に本をあげました。
setting.en: I gave my friend a book. (away from me)

extensions.scene: The heater came the other way, toward you, and English would use the same verb for both. Japanese will not — giving that arrives at your side of the relationship has its own word and cannot borrow the other.
extensions.jp: 友達が本をくれました。
extensions.en: My friend gave me a book — toward me, so くれる.

extensions.scene: The third one you tell from your own end rather than the giver's, which is the receiving verb — and its source takes the particle you would expect to mean a destination.
extensions.jp: 先生に薬をもらいました。
extensions.en: I got medicine from the teacher — に marks the giver.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Apartment hunting again, because the lease is up in March and the agent wants a shortlist by Friday. Every sentence you need is a judgement about a room — big, cheap, cold, far — and the words that carry judgements in Japanese conjugate like verbs rather than sitting still like English adjectives do.
setting.jp: この店は高くないです。

extensions.scene: You saw one on Tuesday that was fine and one on Wednesday that was not, and reporting that needs the past — which the adjective builds itself, out of its own body, with no help from anything else in the sentence.
extensions.en: It was spacious.

extensions.scene: Four shapes to own and two classic wrecks. Adding でした to an adjective is the first, because that ending belongs to nouns. Using the noun negative on it is the second, and both look completely reasonable coming out of English.
extensions.en: It wasn't expensive — not 高いでした, not 高いじゃない.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The second flat is above a bakery on a street with no through traffic, and the word you want for it is one you have known for weeks — except that it behaves like a noun rather than like the words you learned in the last lesson, and it needs a syllable in front of the thing it describes.
setting.jp: 静かな町です。

extensions.scene: You tell the agent what you are after and the same word turns up at the end of the sentence instead of in front of a noun — where the extra syllable vanishes completely, because there is nothing for it to attach to.
extensions.en: This room is quiet — な only before a noun.

extensions.scene: Which family a word belongs to has to be learned with the word, because the spelling lies. Two of the commonest end in the same kana as the other family and belong firmly to this one.
extensions.en: A clean room — きれい ends in い and is な all the same.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: One sentence to describe the flat you want, into a phone, to an agent who has four minutes. You have the adjectives and you have been saying them one at a time in separate sentences, which sounds like a list read out by a machine.
setting.jp: この部屋は広くて明るいです。
setting.en: This room is spacious and bright.

extensions.scene: The one you saw yesterday needs two words from the other family joined together, which uses a different connector — matching the joint to the family is the whole of the rule.
extensions.en: It was quiet and straightforward — で for な-words.

extensions.scene: The chain takes its tense from the end, so the last word makes the whole thing past. And the joint only links qualities pulling the same way — for two that disagree, the sentence needs the but from Step 11.
extensions.jp: 安くて、おいしかったです。
extensions.en: Cheap and good — the final word makes both past.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
明るい and おいしい sit outside the Step 9 bank; both are module examples.

setting.scene: Four months in, and the thing everybody comments on is that the weather has turned and so has your Japanese. Both are changes that happened without anybody doing anything on purpose, which is one verb in Japanese and the it-happens twin of the pair you met in Step 4.
setting.jp: 天気がよくなりました。

extensions.scene: Somebody says the second one to you at the end of a meeting, and it is the same verb doing the same job about a person rather than a season — a change that arrived rather than one anybody performed.
extensions.jp: 日本語が上手になりましたね。
extensions.en: Your Japanese has got good, hasn't it.

extensions.scene: How the word in front joins depends on its family — one drops its last kana and takes a different one, the other takes に — and the commonest adjective in the language is irregular in exactly this spot.
extensions.en: いい is irregular: よくなる, never いくなる.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The staffroom is cold enough that two people are working in coats, and the heater controls are behind your desk. Somebody asks you to do something about it — which is the other twin of the verb you just learned, the one that needs a person to perform it and a thing to perform it on.
setting.jp: 部屋を暖かくしてください。

extensions.scene: You ask the same of the caretaker about the corridor, which nobody has heated since November — the same twin of the same verb, this time as your request, with a doer in the sentence and a thing being done to.
extensions.jp: 部屋を静かにしてください。
extensions.en: Please make the room quiet.

extensions.scene: The pair sit one word apart and mean entirely different things about who is responsible. One says the room warmed up. The other says somebody turned the heating on, and that somebody is in the sentence.
extensions.jp: 部屋が暖かくなりました。
extensions.en: The room warmed up — nobody did it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
暖かい sits outside the Step 9 bank; it is the module's own example.
暖 is outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed. Kept because the word is the module's own example vocabulary for this point.

setting.scene: A restaurant with the whole section, a laminated menu you can read about a third of, and a waiter already standing at your elbow with a pad. The question he asks is the one every restaurant in the country asks, and the answer is a fixed pattern that means neither becoming nor doing but choosing between things.
setting.jp: 私はコーヒーにします。

extensions.scene: Somebody hesitates and you ask them the same question the waiter asked you, which is the shape you will use in every restaurant, ticket office and coffee shop from here on.
extensions.en: What will you have?

extensions.t: One vowel from a different world: にします chooses, になります becomes. コーヒーにします orders a coffee; コーヒーになります is a prophecy. Both are grammatical, which is why the slip goes unnoticed by everyone except the waiter.
extensions.scene: You get one kana wrong and announce, to a waiter holding a pad, that you are going to turn into a coffee. He writes down what you meant, because context is generous, and you hear it a second later.
extensions.en: I will become coffee — one kana away from ordering one.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Somebody has cooked and is asking whether you like it, and the honest answer is not very — which in English is a small negative and in Japanese is a whole grammatical contract. The adverb makes a promise at the front of the sentence that the ending has to keep.
setting.jp: あまり高くないです。

extensions.scene: Later somebody asks about a dish you genuinely do not like, and this is the polite machinery for saying so — not the blunt word for dislike, but this adverb doing social work.
extensions.jp: あまり好きじゃないです。
extensions.en: I don't like it very much.

extensions.scene: Start the sentence with it and forget to finish negative, and the contract breaks halfway. The adverb is a promise of a negative ending, and the next lesson's adverb makes the same promise harder.
extensions.en: あまり高いです is broken — the ending must be negative.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
好き arrives in Step 10; used here as the module's own example.

setting.scene: A meeting in which somebody speaks for six minutes about something you needed to understand, and afterwards asks, kindly, how much of it landed. The honest answer is at the far end of the same dial you learned last lesson, and it makes the same promise about how the sentence has to end.
setting.jp: ぜんぜんわかりません。

extensions.scene: She asks whether it was too fast and you use it again about something else that was entirely absent — the adverb at the front, the negative at the end, the whole distance between them held open.
extensions.jp: ぜんぜん時間がありません。
extensions.en: There's no time at all.

extensions.scene: Then somebody at lunch uses it with a positive and nobody blinks, because casual speech bends this rule daily. Recognise it, enjoy it, and keep your own version negative in anything written or polite.
extensions.en: Totally fine — real, common, and casual only.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
大丈夫 sits outside the Step 9 bank; it appears in the module's own wrinkle and in the Step 8 culture lesson.

setting.scene: Parents' evening again, a year on, and every sentence you say tonight is a judgement with a dial on it. There are four settings on that dial and you have been using one of them for everything, which makes twelve conversations sound like the same conversation.
setting.jp: この映画はとても面白いです。

extensions.scene: For a child who is nearly there rather than entirely there, you need the small setting instead — the same slot in the sentence, one notch down, and a completely different message home.
extensions.en: It's a little difficult.

extensions.scene: What the big one cannot do is go negative. For not very the language changes machinery altogether and reaches for last lesson's adverb, so the full dial runs across two different systems.
extensions.jp: あまり面白くないです。
extensions.en: Not very interesting — とても can't do this job.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
難しい sits outside the Step 9 bank.
難 is outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed. Kept because the word is the module's own example vocabulary for this point.

setting.scene: Two routes to work, and after four months of alternating you finally have an opinion. Somebody in the staffroom asks which is better and the answer is a frame with two slots — and the adjective inside it does not change shape at all, however hard English wants it to.
setting.jp: 電車よりバスのほうが安いです。
setting.en: The bus is cheaper than the train.

extensions.scene: You ask her the same about summer and winter, which is the small talk equivalent of a free square, and the frame goes out exactly as it came in with two new nouns dropped into the slots.
extensions.jp: 夏より冬のほうが好きです。
extensions.en: I prefer winter to summer.

extensions.scene: Asked which of two you prefer, the answer keeps the second half of the frame and drops the first entirely — the thing being compared against has already been said, so it does not need saying again.
extensions.en: I prefer cats — より gone, のほうが stays.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The children have worked out that you will answer questions about yourself, and have moved on from two-way comparisons to outright rankings — favourite food, favourite season, favourite animal, in that order, every lunchtime. Two things compare with last lesson's frame; three or more crown a winner, and crowning needs a different word entirely.
setting.jp: 果物のなかでりんごがいちばん好きです。
setting.en: Of all fruit I like apples best.

extensions.scene: You turn it round on them, which buys four minutes and gets the whole class talking — the group takes one frame, and the thing being crowned takes the particle that has been following 好き around all step.
extensions.jp: 野菜のなかで何がいちばん好きですか。
extensions.en: Which vegetable do you like best?

extensions.scene: The question word in that sentence takes the same particle it took back in Step 1, which has been quietly on duty ever since — and the adjective, again, does no work at all.
extensions.jp: 誰がいちばん上手ですか。
extensions.en: Who is best at it? — question words take が.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A welcome dinner for the new term, and the question going round the table is what music you listen to. The sentence you want has a thing you like sitting in the middle of it, and every instinct you own says that thing is the object of the verb.
setting.jp: 音楽が好きです。

extensions.scene: You ask it back and get it wrong in the other direction, about a food you would rather avoid — because the blunt word for dislike lands far harder in Japanese than its English translation suggests.
extensions.jp: あまり好きじゃないです。
extensions.en: I don't like it much — the polite version of dislike.

extensions.scene: The error is completely predictable and survives a year if nobody corrects it. 好き is not a verb; it is describing a state, and the thing you like is grammatically what does the pleasing.
extensions.en: 音楽を好きです is the classic wreck — が, always.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Four months in, somebody tells you your Japanese is good, and it is not — it is better than it was, which is a different thing. What follows is a small ritual with two moves in it, and the word they used is one you must never point back at yourself.
setting.jp: 妹はピアノが上手です。
setting.en: My sister is good at piano.

extensions.scene: Somebody asks what you are actually good at, and the honest answer needs the modest word instead — the one you use about your own strengths, because the other one aimed inward reads as boasting.
extensions.en: Cooking is my strong suit.

extensions.scene: The second move of the ritual is the deflection, and it is not false modesty so much as the expected next line. Agreeing with the compliment is the move that actually lands badly.
extensions.jp: いえいえ、まだまだです。
extensions.en: Not at all, I've a long way to go.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
料理 and 得意 sit outside the Step 10 bank; 得意 is named in the module's own watch beat.

setting.scene: A parent is explaining something at speed and stops to check whether you are following. There are two words that both come out as understand in English and they are not interchangeable — one is having the information, the other is it making sense, and the negatives split harder than the positives do.
setting.jp: 日本語が少しわかります。

extensions.scene: Somebody asks whether you know a colleague by name, which turns out to be the other verb entirely — that one is about holding a piece of information rather than about anything becoming clear to you.
extensions.en: I know (of) her.

extensions.scene: The particle is the same trap as 好き, one lesson on. It helps to read the verb as is-clear-to-me rather than as understand, because then the が stops looking wrong.
extensions.en: Japanese is clear to me — hence が, not を.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A form for the school newsletter asks about hobbies, and every answer you want is a verb rather than a noun — reading, walking, cooking. Japanese will not let a verb take the particle that 好き demands until something turns the verb into a thing first, and Step 3 promised this job was coming.
setting.jp: 本を読むのが好きです。

extensions.scene: You ask a colleague the same and her answer runs the identical machinery on a different verb — the plain form, then the one syllable that turns it into a noun, then the particle that was waiting for one.
extensions.jp: 歌を歌うのが好きです。
extensions.en: I like singing.

extensions.scene: It only works on the plain form, and the object inside survives — so the sentence ends up carrying two particles doing two entirely different jobs, one inside the noun and one outside it.
extensions.jp: 本を読むのが好きです。
extensions.en: を inside, が outside — 読みますのが is out.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The phone shop again, a year on, and the question is whether the card in your hand will work in their machine. It is a question about capability rather than about anybody's intention, and Japanese builds that into the verb itself rather than adding a word in front of it.
setting.jp: 日本語が少し話せます。
setting.en: I can speak a little Japanese.

extensions.scene: You ask about the card, which is a capability belonging to an object rather than a person — the same form, and the grammar does not care that nobody involved has a will.
extensions.jp: この店でカードが使えますか。
extensions.en: Can I use a card in this shop?

extensions.scene: How the verb bends depends on which family it is in, and the thing you are able to do switches its particle at the same time — from the object marker to the one this whole step has been drumming.
extensions.jp: 朝早く起きられません。
extensions.en: I can't get up early — 起きる → 起きられる, negated.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
早く sits outside the Step 10 bank; from the module's own wrinkle.

setting.scene: Two unrelated particles are about to collide in the same paragraph. One is the が you learned in Step 4, belonging to the twin of a verb that happens by itself. The other is the が this whole step has been handing out to 好き, わかる and the potential form. Same kana, entirely different reasons.
setting.jp: ドアが開きました。

extensions.scene: One sentence later you use the other kind about something you like, and nothing on the page distinguishes them — which is fine as long as you know which of the two you are writing at the time.
extensions.en: I like music — the state-family's が.

extensions.t: The Step 4 self-check still holds and matters more here: を in front of an it-just-happens verb is always an error. What is new is that this step's compositions are full of both がs at once, so naming which one you are using keeps both honest.
extensions.scene: You write a paragraph with four of them in it and two are one kind and two the other. Reading it back, the only way to check is to ask of each one what job it thought it was doing.
extensions.jp: 窓が閉まりました。日本語がわかります。
extensions.en: The window closed. I understand Japanese. Two がs, two reasons.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: This step's real subject is not comparison at all. It is が turning up in exactly the places English swears there should be an object, and the composition ahead is a minefield of them on purpose — every 好き, 上手, 下手 and わかる in anything you write deserves a second look before you hand it in.
setting.jp: 日本語がわかります。

extensions.scene: You check your own newsletter paragraph and find three places where you reached for the object marker out of habit. All three are about states rather than actions, and all three want the other particle.
extensions.jp: 新しいくつがほしいです。
extensions.en: I want new shoes — ほしい takes が too.

extensions.t: One more trap in the same family: 上手 is not used about yourself. 得意 states a strength plainly and modestly; 上手 aimed inward reads as self-praise, whatever the particle is doing.
extensions.scene: The last sentence of the paragraph is about something you are good at, and the particle is right while the word is not — modest about the grammar, immodest about the claim.
extensions.en: Cooking is my strong suit — not 私は料理が上手です.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
くつ and 料理 sit outside the Step 10 bank; くつ is from the module's own example.

setting.scene: The staffroom in August with the windows shut because of the insects and the air conditioning fighting a losing battle. Somebody has to say why they are opening one, and in Japanese the reason goes first and the consequence second — which is the mirror of the English sentence you are translating in your head.
setting.jp: 暑いから、窓を開けました。
setting.en: Because it was hot, I opened the window.

extensions.scene: Ten minutes later you leave early for the clinic, and saying why is the same shape with your own reason in front — the order stops feeling backwards somewhere around the fourth time you build it.
extensions.jp: 頭が痛いから、帰ります。
extensions.en: I've got a headache, so I'm going home.

extensions.scene: Asked directly why, the reason can stand entirely on its own with nothing after it — and note the joint: this one takes a whole finished clause, where the から from Step 7 took a connector form.
extensions.en: Because I'm busy — the reason alone, closed with です.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Leaving before the section head does, for the second time this week, with a genuine reason and no wish to sound like you are asserting it. There are two words for because and they differ in force: one states a reason, the other presents it as circumstance, and workplace exits reach for the second.
setting.jp: 頭が痛いので、帰ります。
setting.en: I'm going home because I have a headache.

extensions.scene: An email to somebody senior about a deadline you will miss, where the softer of the two is doing real work — it hands over a circumstance rather than pushing a justification across the desk.
extensions.jp: 時間がないので、明日します。
extensions.en: There's no time, so I'll do it tomorrow.

extensions.scene: A noun in front of it needs a syllable you would not predict — the same one that turns up before ん in the explanatory form from Step 3, doing exactly the same joining job.
extensions.en: It's raining, so I won't go — 雨なので, never 雨だので.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A restaurant recommendation you want to give honestly, which means saying two things that pull against each other in one sentence. The connector that joins opposing halves is a kana you already know as a particle, doing an entirely unrelated job in an entirely different position.
setting.jp: 高いですが、おいしいです。

extensions.scene: You use the casual cousin of it with the teacher you eat lunch with, which is the same joint one register down and by far the more common of the two in speech.
extensions.en: I'm busy, but I'll go.

extensions.scene: Then it turns up as a cushion in front of a question, meaning almost nothing at all — not contradiction but courtesy, the polite throat-clearing before you ask a stranger for something.
extensions.jp: すみませんが、駅はどこですか。
extensions.en: Excuse me, but where's the station? — が as a cushion.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Writing the first long thing you have written in Japanese — three paragraphs for the school newsletter — and everything you produce comes out as one enormous sentence, because the words you know for but and and then all join clauses. The ones that start new sentences are different words, and mixing them up is the visible learner seam.
setting.jp: 雨でした。でも、出かけました。
setting.en: It was raining. But I went out.

extensions.scene: You break the second paragraph in half and open the new sentence with it, which is the only position it can take — and the paragraph immediately stops sounding like one breath.
extensions.jp: でも、時間がありませんでした。
extensions.en: But there wasn't any time.

extensions.scene: Mid-sentence, the job belongs to the other two words entirely. English uses one word in both positions, so the split has to be watched every single time you join two halves rather than start something new.
extensions.jp: 雨でしたが、出かけました。
extensions.en: Same meaning, joined rather than started — が, not でも.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Somebody recommends a film and you catch the shape of the sentence but not the name inside it, which is the ordinary condition of your life here. The frame that attaches a name to a thing is one pattern — and run backwards it becomes the single most useful question a learner can own.
setting.jp: 「花」という映画を見ました。

extensions.scene: You use it about the place near the station whose name you finally learned, which is the first time all month you have introduced something rather than asked about it.
extensions.jp: 「さくら」という店に行きました。
extensions.en: I went to a shop called Sakura.

extensions.scene: Then the machine runs the other way. Anything you can point at, you can now get the name of — and the answer comes back inside the same frame you asked in.
extensions.jp: これは日本語で何といいますか。
extensions.en: What's this called in Japanese?

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
花 is outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed. Kept because the word is the module's own example vocabulary for this point.

setting.scene: A child has handed nothing in for a week and you have to ask why, in a language where the bare why-question presses considerably harder than its English translation does. The word itself is easy and you have known it since Step 1. The register it lands in, said flat to a twelve-year-old, is the whole of the problem.
setting.jp: どうして遅れましたか。

extensions.scene: You answer one yourself at the end of the day, about the meeting you missed, and the reply comes back in the frame the question set up — the reason, closed off with the ending from two lessons ago.
extensions.jp: 時間がなかったからです。
extensions.en: Because there wasn't time.

extensions.scene: Asked flat, it can land as a demand for justification rather than a question. The explanatory syllable from Step 3 cushions it into curiosity, and in real speech between people it is almost always there.
extensions.jp: どうして遅れたんですか。
extensions.en: Why were you late? — the ん softens the asking.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Half past nine at night in a town where two things are open, and the question is not what you want but whether you want anything at all. Japanese builds indefinite words out of the question words you already own, plus one kana — and the difference between them and the questions they came from is one syllable wide.
setting.jp: 何か食べたいです。

extensions.scene: Somebody asks where you are going on Sunday and the honest answer is nowhere decided yet — which is the same construction built on a different question word, and it works on every one of them.
extensions.en: I'm going somewhere.

extensions.scene: Particles mostly drop off these, and the one-syllable difference decides what kind of answer you are asking for — whether you ate anything is a yes-or-no; what you ate is a list.
extensions.en: Did you eat anything? — a yes/no, not a what.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The newsletter draft comes back from the teacher who checks it with four words changed out of kanji and into kana, and none of them were wrong. Which script a word gets is convention rather than rule, and over-using kanji is the more common learner error — not under-using it.
setting.jp: きれいな部屋です。
setting.en: Conventionally kana, even though 綺麗 exists.

extensions.scene: You rewrite two more of your own on the same principle, and the paragraph stops looking like it was assembled out of a dictionary and starts looking like ordinary writing.
extensions.en: A little difficult — kana, by convention.

extensions.t: This is also why the checker treats script choice as a note rather than an error. A word written in kanji where convention prefers kana is not wrong; it is loud, and loudness is a register problem rather than a grammar one.
extensions.scene: Nothing you wrote would have been marked incorrect by anybody. It simply read as though it had been written by someone with a dictionary open, which after four months it had not been.
extensions.en: Kana here reads as ordinary; kanji would read as formal.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
難しい and 綺麗 sit outside the Step 11 bank; both are from the module's own example.
難 is outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed. Kept because the word is the module's own example vocabulary for this point.

setting.scene: The two particles from Step 2 come back with everything you have learned since standing behind them. The topic set at the front of a sentence carries on through the contrast in the middle of it, which is a thing you could not have seen in Step 2 because you had no contrast to see it with.
setting.jp: この店は高いですが、おいしいです。
setting.en: Topic は carries through the contrast.

extensions.scene: You write your own two-clause sentence about the flat and the topic set at the front holds for both halves without being said twice — which is most of what makes long sentences bearable to read.
extensions.jp: この部屋は広いですが、寒いです。
extensions.en: This room is spacious but cold.

extensions.t: The test has not changed since Step 2: if the sentence answers which one, it takes が; if it names what you are already discussing, it takes は. What has changed is the length of the sentences you are testing.
extensions.scene: The paragraph you have just written has six of them in it, and every single one still answers the same question the Step 2 test asked. The rule did not grow any more complicated; the sentences around it did.
extensions.jp: 誰が来ましたか。— 田中さんが来ました。
extensions.en: Who came? — Tanaka did. Question and answer, both が.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Step 3 told you to delete the word for I, and you took it to heart, and now you have deleted one that was doing a job. A describing clause needs its own subject inside it — and inside that clause, the subject takes the other particle, which is the part nobody warns you about.
setting.jp: 私が好きなスポーツはテニスです。
setting.en: 私 stays: the clause needs its own subject, and it takes が.

extensions.scene: You write another one about a book rather than a sport, and the same structure needs the same word in the same place — not because the sentence is about you, but because the clause inside it is.
extensions.jp: 私が読んだ本は面白かったです。
extensions.en: The book I read was interesting.

extensions.t: The over-correction is real and it produces sentences that are wrong in a new way. Deleting every 私 is as mechanical as inserting every 私 was; what changed in Step 3 was the default, not the rule.
extensions.scene: Reading back a paragraph you pruned last week, two sentences have lost the subject of a clause — and now they describe somebody unspecified doing something you had meant to claim as your own.
extensions.en: It's food I made — drop 私が and the cook goes missing.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
スポーツ, テニス, 面白い, 料理 sit outside the Step 11 bank; スポーツ/テニス are from the module's own example.

setting.scene: A planning meeting where you have an opinion and no wish to state it as fact, because you have been here five months and the people around the table have been here twenty years. Japanese puts the whole thought first and the reporting verb last, which is the same back-to-front shape as describing a noun with a clause.
setting.jp: この店は高いと思います。
setting.en: I think this shop is expensive.

extensions.scene: Somebody asks what you reckon about the timing and you build your own — the clause in front stays plain however polite the ending gets, which is the whole division of labour.
extensions.jp: 時間がないと思います。
extensions.en: I think there isn't time.

extensions.t: です never appears in front of と思います — 高いですと思います is wrong; it is 高いと思います. Nouns and な-adjectives take だ instead: 学生だと思います. And Japanese negates the thought rather than the reporting, so 来ないと思います is what gets said, not 来ると思いません.
extensions.scene: Your first attempt is polite in the middle, where the politeness does not belong, and your second negates the wrong half of the sentence — both of which sound like careful English and like nothing anybody here says.
extensions.en: I think he won't come — negate the thought, not the thinking.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Your name got read out in the morning meeting in connection with a form you had not been told about, and telling that story afterwards needs a shape where the thing happens to you rather than by you. English mostly avoids this by rearranging the sentence; Japanese bends the verb.
setting.jp: 私は先生に名前を聞かれました。
setting.en: The teacher asked me my name.

extensions.scene: You use it about something smaller and more annoying — the umbrella that went from the stand by the door — and the person responsible does not have to appear in the sentence at all.
extensions.en: My umbrella was taken.

extensions.scene: Then the version English has no grammar for whatsoever: the weather doing something to you. Japanese lets an event happen to a person grammatically, and the sentence carries the grievance without a single word of complaint in it.
extensions.en: I got rained on — the suffering passive.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
かさ and 取る sit outside the Step 12 bank; かさ arrives in Step 13.
取 is outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed. Kept because the word is the module's own example vocabulary for this point.

setting.scene: A trip with two colleagues and one of them wants a phone call when you land, which is a sentence with a condition in front of it and an instruction behind. Japanese has four words for if and this stage teaches two of them — and only one of the two can be followed by a request.
setting.jp: 時間があったら、行きます。
setting.en: If I have time, I'll go.

extensions.scene: You make the promise yourself, to the colleague who asked for it, which is exactly the sentence this whole lesson exists for: a condition in front, and something you are undertaking to do about it behind.
extensions.jp: 日本に着いたら、電話してください。
extensions.en: Call me when you get to Japan.

extensions.scene: The other one from this step cannot carry that. It describes something automatic, so a request behind it makes no sense — and the remaining two ifs are deferred to Stage 2, which is a deferral rather than an omission.
extensions.jp: 冬になると、寒くなります。
extensions.en: When winter comes it gets cold — と is automatic, no requests.
